tasks.title: Latch driven by a clock
tasks.statement: The clock signal CLK is just a wire that keeps rising to 1 and falling to 0. Feed it to the enable input of a D latch: while CLK = 1 the latch is open and follows D; when CLK = 0 it holds.
tasks.hint: This is the ordinary D latch from the previous section: S = D·CLK, R = NOT-D·CLK, then two cross-coupled NORs. CLK plays the role of enable E.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Clock high: D = 1, CLK = 1. The latch is open, Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Clock falls: CLK = 0. The latch is locked, Q holds 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Change D to 0 while the clock is low: Q does not react.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Clock rises: the latch opens and takes D = 0. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Without lowering CLK, change D to 1: Q follows it immediately!
spec_text./steps/5/text: And back, D = 0: Q follows again. While the clock is high the latch is “transparent”: data flies right through it.
spec_text./formula: CLK = 1: Q = D; CLK = 0: Q holds
spec_text./success: It works, but there is a problem: while CLK is high, data “flies” straight through the latch. If the output of one such latch feeds the input of another, the signal will slip through both, or the whole chain, within a single high clock. We need memory that captures the value exactly at the MOMENT the clock changes.

tasks.title: Latch open on low clock
tasks.statement: Build a mirror latch: open while CLK = 0 (follows D) and locked when CLK = 1 (holds). This is half of the future flip-flop.
tasks.hint: You need an inverter on the clock: E = NOT-CLK. The rest is the same D latch (two ANDs, NOT on D, two NORs), only NOT-CLK goes into the “keys” instead of CLK.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Clock low: the latch is open. D = 1 → Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Raise CLK: the latch is locked and holds 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Change D to 0 while the clock is high: Q does not react.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Lower CLK: the latch opens and takes D = 0. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/4/text: While the clock is low, D = 1 passes straight to Q.
spec_text./formula: E = NOT-CLK; CLK = 0: Q = D; CLK = 1: Q holds
spec_text./success: One latch is open at CLK = 1, the other at CLK = 0. They are never open at the same time. Put them one after the other and data can pass only one of the two at a time; that is the secret of the flip-flop.

tasks.title: Edge-triggered D flip-flop
tasks.statement: Place the latches one after another: the “master” is open at CLK = 0 and takes D, the “slave” is open at CLK = 1 and takes the value from the master. Output Q changes only at the moment CLK rises from 0 to 1, on the EDGE. Q and nQ are the outputs of the slave latch.
tasks.hint: The master is from the previous exercise (E = NOT-CLK): NOT on CLK, NOT on D, two ANDs with NOT-CLK, two NORs. The slave is a latch with E = CLK, whose data D is the master's output Q. Take Q and nQ from the slave. About ten gates in total.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Apply D = 1 with CLK = 0. The master latch is open and has taken 1, but output Q is not yet defined: the slave is locked and holds nothing so far.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Edge: CLK 0 → 1. The master closed with a one inside, the slave opened and put it on Q.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Without lowering CLK, change D to 0: the master is locked, Q does not react. No more transparency!
spec_text./steps/3/text: Lower CLK (falling edge): Q is still 1, and the master has already taken D = 0.
spec_text./steps/4/text: A new edge with D = 0: a zero rolls out onto Q.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Change D to 1 while CLK is high: Q holds 0 until the next edge.
spec_text./formula: Q ← D at the moment CLK: 0 → 1
spec_text./success: This is the D flip-flop, the main building block of synchronous circuits. It “photographs” D once per clock, at the moment of the edge, and holds the snapshot for the whole period, whatever the inputs do. Building it unlocked a ready-made DFF gate in the palette: in the next exercises you will place it with one click.

tasks.title: Divide by two
tasks.statement: Connect the flip-flop's output back to its own D input through an inverter: D = NOT-Q. Each CLK edge will flip Q. Press “Tick”: Q should go 1, 0, 1, 0. A ready-made flip-flop starts at zero on power-up.
tasks.hint: Two elements: DFF and NOT. The DFF output goes to the NOT input, and the NOT output goes back to the flip-flop's D input. Feed the clock to the flip-flop's CLK.

spec_text./steps/0/text: First tick: Q was 0, D = NOT-Q = 1, so Q becomes 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Second tick: now D = 0, and Q goes back to 0.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Fourth tick: 0. Q runs at half the clock speed.
spec_text./formula: D = NOT-Q; Q toggles on every edge
spec_text./success: The frequency of Q is half the clock's: this is a frequency divider, also a one-bit counter (0, 1, 0, 1…). Note that the flip-flop's output feeds its own input and everything still works, whereas in a latch such a loop would run away into oscillation. The edge gives exactly one step.

tasks.title: Register with load enable
tasks.statement: Keep the value while there is no command, and store a new one only when LD = 1: on a CLK edge Q takes D if LD = 1, and stays the same if LD = 0. Every processor register has a load enable.
tasks.hint: Put a multiplexer in front of the flip-flop's D input: D' = LD·D OR NOT-LD·Q. With LD = 0 the flip-flop receives its own output, so the value does not change. The flip-flop's output Q returns to the multiplexer.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Write: D = 1, LD = 1, then a tick. Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: D = 0, but LD = 0, so writing is disabled. After a tick Q stays 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: LD = 1 and D = 0: a zero is written. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/3/text: D = 1, LD = 0: writing is disabled again. Q = 0.
spec_text./success: A “myself or the new value” multiplexer is a standard trick: every bit of a register with load enable is built this way. In a processor, the LD signal comes from the address decoder, which opens writing only for the right register.

tasks.title: Synchronous reset
tasks.statement: Add a clear input CLR to the register: when CLR = 1, Q becomes 0 on the next edge (otherwise Q takes D). The reset is “synchronous”: by itself, without a clock, nothing changes.
tasks.hint: Data for the flip-flop: D' = D·NOT-CLR. While CLR = 1, the flip-flop's input is zero, and the next edge will store it.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Write a one: D = 1, CLR = 0, tick. Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Turn on CLR = 1 without a tick: Q is still 1. The reset waits for an edge.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Tick: clear beats data. Q = 0 even though D = 1.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Release CLR and tick: D = 1 is written again. Q = 1.
spec_text./success: A synchronous reset is safer than an asynchronous one: it also obeys the clock, so there is no “zeroing in the middle of a period”. At power-up a processor holds CLR = 1 for a few clocks, and its entire state becomes zero.

tasks.title: Four-bit register
tasks.statement: One word is four bits D3…D0. Build the register: one flip-flop per digit, with a common clock. On a CLK edge the register captures the whole number at once; between edges it holds it, however the inputs change.
tasks.hint: Four DFF elements. Their D inputs are D3…D0, their clock inputs are all connected to one CLK, and their outputs go to Q3…Q0. The clock wire branches.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Set the number 1011 and tick: the register has stored 1011.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Change the inputs to 0100 but give no tick: the register holds the old 1011.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Tick: the whole number updated at once, to 0100.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Set 1111 and tick: the register holds 1111.
spec_text./formula: Qi ← Di on every CLK edge
spec_text./success: A register is just N flip-flops with a common clock. In a 64-bit processor each register has 64 flip-flops, and they all switch at once, on one edge. The common clock is what makes the circuit synchronous: “everything changes only on the signal”.

tasks.title: Shift register
tasks.statement: Chain four flip-flops: Din goes into the first, the first's output into the second, and so on. On every edge the number shifts by one digit, and a new bit Din enters on the right. Q0 is the “freshest” bit, Q3 is the oldest.
tasks.hint: Four DFFs with their clock inputs tied together. Din → D of the first; Q of the first → D of the second; Q of the second → D of the third; Q of the third → D of the fourth. Q0 is the output of the first flip-flop, Q3 of the fourth.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Din = 1, tick: a one entered Q0. Register: 0001.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Din = 0, tick: the one shifted to Q1, a zero entered Q0. Register: 0010.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Din = 1, tick: shift, and a new one in Q0. Register: 0101.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Din = 0, tick: the high bit fell off the edge and vanished. Register: 0110.
spec_text./success: All flip-flops sample their inputs simultaneously, on one edge, so the signal advances exactly ONE step per clock. With latches in their place, the number would “fly” through the whole chain in a single high clock. Shift registers convert serial data to parallel and back: this is how serial ports work.

tasks.title: Two-bit counter
tasks.statement: Build a modulo-4 counter: after every edge Q1 Q0 grows by one: 00, 01, 10, 11, then 00 again. This is the “incrementer” from the adders section, closed into a register.
tasks.hint: You need two flip-flops. The low one: D0 = NOT-Q0 (flips every clock). The high one: D1 = Q1⊕Q0 (flips only when Q0 = 1). The flip-flop outputs Q0 and Q1 return to the logic inputs.

spec_text./steps/3/text: Fourth tick: 11 → 00. Overflow: counting goes around in a circle.
spec_text./success: A counter is a register plus “+1” on its input. If you add an arbitrary number instead of one, you get an accumulator (the finale of this section). And if you count instruction addresses, you get the program counter: the “heart” of a processor, stepping through the program clock by clock.

tasks.title: Counter with enable
tasks.statement: A counter that counts only while EN = 1. With EN = 0 an edge changes nothing: Q1 Q0 stay as they were. This lets you “stop” counting without touching the clock.
tasks.hint: The same counter, but “+1” is replaced by “+EN”: D0 = Q0⊕EN; D1 = Q1⊕(Q0·EN). With EN = 0 each XOR with zero returns the same value, so the digit does not change.

spec_text./steps/2/text: EN = 0, tick: the counter did not move and is still 10.
spec_text./success: This is also an adder: EN (0 or 1) is added to the value. All that remains is to add not 0 or 1 but any two-bit number, and that will be an accumulator. Mind the enable: a counter “stop” in a processor means waiting for input, pauses and debugging.

tasks.title: Johnson counter
tasks.statement: A clever counter with two flip-flops and ONE inverter: Q1 takes the previous Q0, and Q0 takes NOT-Q1. The states go around a circle: 00 → 01 → 11 → 10 → 00. Between neighboring states only one bit changes.
tasks.hint: This is a two-flip-flop shift register whose input is the NOT of the last output: D0 = NOT-Q1, D1 = Q0. Output Q1 goes both to the output and to the inverter.

spec_text./steps/3/text: Fourth tick: 10 → 00. The circle is closed.
spec_text./success: A code in which neighboring numbers differ by one bit is called a Gray code. It is handy where transition safety matters: there is no moment when two bits change out of step, so the counter cannot be “read” wrongly. Shaft position sensors work exactly this way.

tasks.title: Accumulator
tasks.statement: The finale of the section is the “brain” of the arithmetic cycle. A two-bit register Q1 Q0 holds the accumulated number. On every edge the input number IN1 IN0 is added to it (modulo 4) and the sum is written back into the register. The adder and the register are closed into a loop.
tasks.hint: The two-bit adder from the previous section: S0 = Q0⊕IN0, carry c = Q0·IN0, S1 = Q1⊕IN1⊕c. Feed sums S0 and S1 to D of two flip-flops, and outputs Q0 and Q1 back to the adder's input. The high carry is simply unused.

spec_text./steps/3/text: Change IN to 10 (that is, 2) and tick: 3 + 2 = 5, which does not fit in two bits, leaving 01.
spec_text./formula: Q ← Q + IN (mod 4) on every edge
spec_text./success: That is a whole computer in miniature: the ALU computes, the register stores, the clock sets the rhythm. Connect a program memory to the IN input and you get a processor: every clock it takes the next number and updates the accumulated result. What remains is to build the whole ALU and teach the circuit to choose an operation.
